And of course, this This conference serves to amplify youth-led priorities, which we will be hearing from you, experiences and recommendations on the thematic issues under the committee's purview. As chair of the Third Committee, it is indeed my privilege to be able to convene this event, the first of its kind. As a space for an open dialogue between member states, young people, civil society on the issue of youth. This event happens as we mark the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, the Pact for the Future, and of course commemorates the 30th anniversary of the World Programme of Action for Youth. This milestone challenges us to renew our collective effort to strengthen our multilateral framework. With more than 1.2 billion youth around the world, the future generation indeed holds immense potential. They are our future leaders, changemakers, influencers, and so much more. Let me express our thanks to Ms. Daphne Lawrence. I now invite Ms. Deanne Keta Executive Director of the United Nations Population Fund, to deliver a statement. The floor is yours.

Thank you so much, Mr. Chair. Your Excellency, distinguished guests, esteemed UN colleagues, dear young partners here in the room and online, Thank you. On the— at the eve of the Girl Child Day, I really would like to thank you, Mr. Chair, for inviting me to speak at the first-ever youth event on the Third Committee. What a powerful demonstration of meaningful intergenerational engagement and an important opportunity to put institutional weight behind our commitment to engage with all the youth.
Thank you.

The important question for me here is, who is being left behind? And how would we know who is left behind? In the largest generation of young people of the world that we have ever seen, too many young people are being overlooked. If an adolescent girl in a remote village might be at risk of child marriage, can be invisible to us, exercising her rights is all but totally impossible. If she isn't seen, she can't be reached. If a young person with a disability lacks access to the services they need or is displaced by a climate disaster, their dignity is often the first casualty. Structural and intersecting barriers such as gender inequality, discrimination, and poverty continue to hold back young people in the most vulnerable circumstances. And those young people are not just left behind, they are being pushed aside.

So being in this room today is already a privilege.

So what can we do with you? We need to rally together to ensure that every young person everywhere can live in full equality, free from harm, and with the hope of future possibilities. Leaving no one behind is not a slogan. It underpins everything that we do at UNFP in our program's work. From directing financial resources to young people who face the most acute barriers, making young people partners in the planning and implementation of our program, and supporting youth-led organizations, we are with you. And you are never alone. And, you know, the— probably young people, this is the only subject we have to work as a UN together. Whether it's the Youth Affairs Office, whether it's UNDESA, ILO, UNICEF, UNDP, I can cite all UN agencies. We need to work together if we want to reach out to you. Thank you. So investing in you all is not really a choice, it's an imperative. You are invaluable experts and understand the need of your communities. This is why in this first dialogue with the Third Committee, that is such an important committee for the UN, we need to be very intentional about shifting resources in this very difficult resource time. And shifting the power to youth-led and youth-focused organizations, including movements, networks led by young women, and feminist organizations. We are committed to empowering all of you so that you can realize your full potential. We have— and I will finish on that— a very dedicated adolescent and youth strategy: My Body, My Life, and My World. Which is our commitment to you. It hinges on those 3 interconnected pillars. First, my body. It's about yourself. It's about ensuring young people can make informed, autonomous choices about their bodies and access sexual reproductive healthcare, which is fundamental to health and human dignity. The second, my life. It's about who you partner with. It's about accessing services. It's about equipping young people with the knowledge, the skills, and opportunity to thrive. And third, my world. It's about your environment, promoting youth participation and leadership, supporting young people in humanitarian settings, and advancing the youth peace and security agenda. It's really about that. So from ICPD to the Pact of the Future to the resolution of the Third Committee, We stand with you by co-creating programs and look forward to contributing more than ever onto the Third Committee work, and we affirm that the United Nations is moving in the right direction towards a greater inclusivity and participation. I thank you.

I thank the Executive Director of the United Nations Population Fund for Thank you very much for her statement. I would like to invite Dr. Philippe Paulier, Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs, to deliver a statement. The floor is yours.

Thank you very much and good afternoon to everyone. I'm very pleased to be here with all of you and I'd like to start by thanking the Third Committee Chair Ambassador for hosting us and for convening this meeting, to the Third Committee Secretariat, our colleagues from DGACM that are always supporting every intergovernmental process, to the Major Group of 4 Children and Youth for inviting all of us, So, Jugradna and Sameh, thank you. And on your behalf, thank you to everyone that builds MGCY as a platform, which is a collective one. And of course, I'm very honored to be in this panel also with these 3 powerful women that lead in the UN, you know, Diane, Cynthia, and Björk, who I admire a lot, and I learn from them every day.
Thank you.

Every day, and and I think it's a it's a clear example of how leadership looks like in the UN in terms of really being very diverse and coming from very different parts of the world, having a strong and a big part of our leadership women. Powerful women that are leading and changing the UN, and hopefully we'll see this also in the new cycle of our next Secretary-General, but especially very, very committed to young people and putting young people at the centre, you know, and I think that's the progress we're seeing in the UN system, and that's something we'll continue to see in the upcoming, you know, together, because this agenda is moving forward because of the advocacy of young people, and the agency of young people. The truth is that today's generation of youth, you know, is carrying the weight of multiple and overlapping crises. Crises related to economic shocks, rising emissions and the climate crisis, conflicts affecting the most always children, youth, and women. And in this very special day also of Mental Health Awareness Day, a very silent mental health epidemic, you know, which is really eroding the hope for our future, and it's also eroding all of the Sustainable Development Goals. And these crises are happening also in, in a very complex political moment for our humanity, you know, where we unfortunately are seeing in many parts of the world shrinking civic spaces, you know, disinformation that spreads. But in this world, young people are not being silent, you know, they're actually taking action. And we are seeing this in multiple parts of the world, both on the digital space, but mainly on the streets, demanding for accountability and pushing our institutions to change. 2 weeks ago, exactly 2 weeks ago, or almost exactly, for the very first time during a high-level week of the UN General Assembly, there was a high-level meeting focusing on young people. It was in commemoration of the 30th anniversary of the World Programme of Action for Youth, that global and common framework that the UN has when it's about approaching youth and supporting youth. But for the UN, it was very important that this was not only an intergovernmental space, it was also an opportunity to really mobilize young people and to bring young people's perspectives and voices, you know. And that's why, with multiple partners of the UN family and with civil society, we were able to push for an exercise of decentralized foresight initiatives before this high-level meeting, so we can build on this high-level meeting also with the voices coming from different parts of the world. And in a very short period between July and August, we were able to mobilize almost 75,000 young people from 182 countries that co-led these dialogues with UN partners, with civil society partners, with governments in some parts of the world, you know, sharing their realities but also putting an emphasis on the future they want to see. And what was the lesson of this exercise for us? Because it's really about how we learn from any of these initiatives. The lesson is that when, from an institutional perspective, we adapt to young people's reality and not the other way around, participation flourishes. Is that when we meet young people where they are, participation flourishes. The renewal of multilateralism will happen where young people are, and young people are in their classrooms, in their community halls, they are on the online spaces, and in many, many informal gatherings across the world. So of course, this critical— and these spaces are very important to make these structural transformations, but it's also about how we go to meet young people where they are. So just to end, I want to make 3 points in terms of how we also believe and how we are trying also to use these forums and spaces to make these structural transformations. The first point is really We cannot promote any of this participation if we don't secure fundamental rights. We cannot expect participation from those that are struggling to survive, you know. We must ensure access to education, to decent jobs, to healthcare, to housing, and to social protection. And we must secure safety when young people express themselves, and we must secure safety for young people to be who they are, defending especially those traditionally left behind. The second is we need to continue to institutionalize meaningful participation because, you know, it's not about events on the margins of the decision-making bodies. It's actually bringing young people into the main and the core of these decision-making bodies and hopefully dreaming about bringing these meaningful and decision-making bodies to young people are. And the third point, it's really about investing, you know. We cannot really do anything of this if there is not secure funding, you know. And, you know, the return of investment about investing in youth-led solutions, it's clearly higher. Than investing in post-conflict, investing in the consequences. So the call, again, as in every platform, is really to put the emphasis there. So for those member states in the room, I think that it's also a recognition, a positive one, that we're moving in the right direction, you know. So I hope that this high-level meeting on youth, where we saw, you know, almost 150 member states in the room, 13 heads of state, almost 90 ministers, not only youth ministers, ministers of foreign affairs, ministers of finance, ministers of climate, is just the beginning, you know. When we bring civil society, as it happened, you know, with 600 civil society representatives participating, we're building a much more inclusive and effective multilateral platform, you know. So I hope we don't need to wait 30 more years to have a high-level meeting on youth during the high-level week. So thank you very much.

I would like to express my thanks to the Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs for a very inspiring statement. Let me turn the microphone to Ms. Cynthia Samuel-Olanjuwon, Special Representative of the International Labour Organization to the United Nations. to deliver a statement. The floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Chair, and thank you for pronouncing my name so well. Excellencies, youth delegates, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, colleagues, friends, I thank the Chair of the UNGA Third Committee for convening this pertinent and very timely conversation on intergenerational solutions for an inclusive future. I really thank the Chair and all those mentioned by Philippe for including the ILO in this discussion, and we're really pleased to work closely with DESA, with the UN Youth Office, with UNFPA, and other UN partners to move this agenda forward. This is not just talk, it's commitment, it's dedication to working with you and all the critical stakeholders to move the needle. Talk, as they say, is very cheap. We don't want the cheap stuff. We really want to work together to move the needle. I'd like to reflect on 3 key issues. First, let's look at the data. According to the recent ILO report on the state of social justice, the world is wealthier, healthier, and better educated when compared to 30 years ago when we held the World Summit for Social Development in Copenhagen. Some of the key achievements include the reduction of child labor from 20.6% to 7.8%, reduction of extreme poverty from 39% to 10%, the reduction of working poverty from 27.9% to 6.9%, achieving social protection coverage for more than 50% of the world's population. That report also highlights that transitions to greener and digital economies are opening new avenues for youth employment. That's the good news. But this good news coexists with persistent challenge. The top 1% control 20% of income and 38% of wealth. While we have also seen improvements in job numbers, 1 in 5 young people worldwide are not in employment, they are not in education, they are not in training. For too many young women and men, the transition from school to work remains a story of lost potential. Young women are nearly 3 times more likely than young men to be in this category, and this is an alarming reminder that gender inequalities continue to hold back young women's progress in the labor market. Even those who find work, it's often in temporary, low-paid or insecure work, and half of young workers are in informal or short-term jobs with no social protection, no hope of upward mobility, referencing the hope that was emphasized in the first presentation that we listened to. It's no surprise then that many young people feel anxious about their future. Mental health and well-being remain the main victim here. Second, these realities reflect deeper societal transformations. In 2018, for the first time ever, there were more people aged 65 and above than children under 5, and by 2080, the number of people over 65 will surpass those under 18. People are living longer, they're living healthier, and many societies are aging rapidly. Older workers are staying longer in the labor force, some by choice, some out of necessity. However, this is not a universal story. Africa's population is booming. With a median age of 19 compared to nearly 40 in North America. This youthquake— not an earthquake— this youthquake is both an opportunity and a challenge, making it crystal clear that creating decent work for Africa's youth is essential, not only for the future of the global economy but for social justice. We need intergenerational solidarity. We need policies that balance the needs of an aging population with the aspirations of the youth, creating a virtuous cycle with each generation supporting the other. Third, and the last area of focus, we need effective collaboration not only across generations, but among all relevant stakeholders for lasting progress. The upcoming Second World Summit for Social Development, which will take place next month in Doha, presents a generational opportunity to refocus our efforts and elevate the social dimension of sustainable development. I'm really pleased to note that the draft political declaration underscores the foundational role of decent work for social development, and it includes commitments to improve the labor market outlook for young and older people, notably through intergenerational knowledge transfer in the workplace. It also includes efforts to enhance the inclusiveness and responsiveness of skill systems to evolving labor market needs. Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, colleagues and friends, the ILO's unique tripartite structure brings together governments, representatives of workers, representatives of business, and offers us a practical example of inclusive governance in shaping global policy. Through the Global Initiative on Decent Jobs for Youth, the UN's first-ever system-wide effort on youth employment, over 100 partners are mobilizing action across sectors, across regions, including driving impact in the digital, the green, and the care economies. As I end, it's important to reiterate that when young people are at the table, policies become sharper, Policies become more relevant. Policies are more equitable. The future of work, and indeed the future of our societies, depends on us working strategically together and in solidarity. I thank you.

I express my thanks to the Special Representative of the ILO to the United Nations for her statement. Thank you very much, Chair. Good afternoon. And thank you again to the Chair of the Third Committee for bringing us together, not least bringing us together with young people to enable us to listen to the very important views that young people bring to the discussions that we have here at the UN and today under the theme Building Intergenerational Solutions for an Inclusive Future. So the 3 speakers before me, I think, have said it all. Put the compelling case for youth involvement, and I don't think I need to tell anyone in this room that that's important. You know it very well. We've had dialogue and interactions before, and I always appreciated the strong voices of the youth always pushing us with very relevant, concrete messages on— so that we as the UN system can work together to be better and to be able to address the real needs and real challenges that you see in your daily lives. So we've heard a lot about that. I'll talk a little bit about the work that we do here at the UN and the engagement of young people there, because we know how young people really are the key to the work of the Third Committee. The discussions that happen in the Third Committee You know, from social development and human rights to inclusion and equality, it does, of course, directly shape the realities and lives of young people and future generations. At the same time, we also know that you are already leading those efforts and driving solutions to turn Global Goals into tangible progress. Where I sit in UN DESA— DESA means the Department of Economic and Social Affairs here at the UN Secretariat— and we work to advance youth inclusion in intergovernmental processes, and we recognize that that meaningful participation of young people in decision-making is essential to building those more inclusive policies that we work on. One of the key ways that we do this is through managing the UN Youth Delegate Program.

I met some of the youth delegates earlier this week, and I see some of you in this room. It's great to see you.

That program provides young people with a formal channel to engage in UN intergovernmental work as members of their national delegations. You don't get closer to policymaking than that. And that, I think, is an inspiring demonstration exactly of how young people, governments, civil society organizations, and the UN can work together to shape and act on shared priorities. And the energy and the ideas that emerged from the Youth Forum continue to guide initiatives Like the event today. It is the first time that we meet with young people under the auspices of the Third Committee, and that doesn't come by itself. It came because young people pushed for it.

So I'd like to thank you for that.

And we would like to keep working to ensure that youth perspectives remain at the heart of the UN's work, including here in the Third Committee. Let me mention briefly also how this year is also a milestone moment, because 2025 does mark the 30th anniversary of the World Programme of Action for Youth, as we heard earlier, and I think it's such a good thing we should repeat it. I mean, again, we had a great event a couple of weeks ago to commemorate that. That Programme of Action is a framework that has guided global efforts on youth development for those 3 decades. Looking ahead to the Second World Summit for Social Development in November in Qatar, as Cynthia also talked about, we see how youth voices will continue to be critical in advancing social development. In 1995, at the First World Social Summit, a number of very important topics were adopted, discussed and adopted among member states that keep shaping the way we do social development today. For example, the whole concept of decent work. Now we take it for granted.

We could not—

we did not take it for granted in '95. I should tell you, I know because I was there. I was a youth delegate at the Social Summit in 1995. Pushing for some of these questions that, you know, that we now see translated into policies, into realities, in communities all over the world. So it, you know, it matters and it means something what you do as young people and how you put your issues into the discussions that we are having. So today's event is part of that continuum. It's a reminder that inclusive intergenerational dialogue strengthens not only the work of this committee, but also the broader efforts to build trust in multilateralism. So by listening and by working alongside young people, we can put forward policies that are more responsive, more equitable, and future-ready. Thank you. Thank you.

It generated our Common Agenda, the Pact for the Future, and many subsequent processes. The UN@80 cannot take away that promise. It must strengthen and not backslide the work that is being done by UN agencies, especially UN agencies in the region and countries on youth issues. The reforms must not affect staff especially working on youth and civil society issues, and major groups and other stakeholders must have direct ways to input to the process that is being undertaken. Excellencies, meaningful youth engagement has to continue to move from theory to action. We continue to embrace diversity in which young people organize on local level.
